title: Choice Overload
description: When faced with too many options, people freeze, make worse choices, or walk away entirely. More is not always better.
shortDescription: When faced with too many options, people freeze, make worse choices, or walk away entirely. More is not always better.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: When faced with too many options, people freeze, make worse choices, or walk away entirely. More is not always better.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A supermarket has 47 types of pasta sauce. You stand there for two minutes, then grab the one you always get, or leave without any.
A streaming service catalogue is so large you scroll for 20 minutes, watch nothing, and turn off the TV.
An online store offers 200 dress options; you get decision fatigue and buy nothing, or later regret what you bought.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Defaulting to a known brand even if it’s not the best.
Feeling relieved when someone narrows it down to three choices.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “There are too many to choose from.”
“I’ll come back to it.” (and never does)

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re spending more time choosing than the decision is worth.
You’re feeling anxious or irritated by a menu or product list.
You keep putting off a small purchase because comparing is exhausting.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Humans have limited working memory and energy for comparison. Each additional option increases the cognitive load until it exceeds capacity. The fear of making a suboptimal choice (maximizing) amplifies the paralysis.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: For personal decisions, limit yourself to three to five options before comparing.
If you’re selling or presenting, offer no more than three choices.
Define your “must‑haves” first to filter options quickly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Thinking more choice always equals more freedom. It can equal more paralysis.
Blaming yourself for indecision rather than recognizing the environment is overloaded.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A jam‑tasting booth in a supermarket offered 24 flavors; many people stopped, but only 3% bought. When they offered 6 flavors, 30% bought (Iyengar & Lepper, 2000). The smaller set made deciding easy.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: A decision that doesn’t get made is often worse than a slightly imperfect one. Cut the list, then choose.
